proposition: Ninety-nine is not a fact about forts. It is a general-purpose Rigvedic quantity that forts are one of at least a dozen things to take.
evidence_for: The expression occurs in 19 stanzas. Forts take it in 6 - under a third. The other 13 uses are rivers (1.32.14, 10.104.8), a retinue (1.53.9), Vr̥tras (1.84.13), rivers or venom-stayers (1.191.13), arms (2.14.4), horses (4.48.4), a serpent's coils (5.29.6), ramparts (6.47.2), unnamed broken things (9.61.1), gifts (10.39.10), the mighty (10.49.8) and oblations (10.98.10). Nothing links that list except the number. RV 10.104.8 carries the expression counting streams AND the epithet pūrbhít 'fort-breaker' in the same stanza, which is the cleanest single case.
evidence_against: The number does not float free of narrative: 99 and 100 sort to Divodāsa, Atithigva and Śambara, while 7 goes with Purukutsa and the Pūru in all four of their passages (PUR4J finding 5). A quantity used for twelve kinds of object is still doing something when it is chosen, and this row does not say it is meaningless. Nor is 19 a large denominator: a distribution over 19 stanzas supports a modest claim about usage, not a law.
what_it_does_not_establish: It does not establish that no Rigvedic fort count records anything historical. A formulaic number can be attached to a remembered event, and one of the six could be. It does not establish anything about WHY ninety-nine - a decimal-adjacent maximum, a one-short-of-a-hundred completion (two of the six add 'the hundredth'), and a stock epic quantity are all live and none is tested here.
falsifier: Falsified by a count outside the stock - a 23 or a 41 - attached to a fort, which would show the corpus can state an arbitrary number and chooses not to. Weakened if the twelve non-fort uses prove to cluster by book, poet or stratum, which would make them a local mannerism rather than a corpus-wide formula. That test was not run.
notes: This SUPERSEDES nothing and CORRECTS nothing in PUR4J-I-01, which reached the compatible conclusion from one control case. It widens the base from 1 to 12 and is recorded separately because the widening is this unit's, and because a reading that survives a twelvefold larger control set is a different evidentiary object from one that rests on a single stanza.

proposition: The corpus gives no positive lexical evidence that a púr- was a brick-built city, and no evidence that it was not. The two absences that look decisive are not.
evidence_for: No lemma is glossed 'brick' or 'city' against a 91.7% lemma / 78.98% token denominator (DJ-008). Grassmann's own gloss of púr- is an earthwork - 'Wall aus Steinen und Lehm, Verschanzung, Palisade' - not a city. 67.5% of simplex tokens are accusative and 3.6% locative: the commonest thing a púr does is be the object of a verb of breaking (DJ-006). The corpus has abundant settlement vocabulary that is NOT púr- (DJ-012).
evidence_against: THIS IS THE HALF THAT MUST NOT BE DROPPED. (1) DJ-009 types the brick absence NOT PRODUCED: a liturgical praise corpus that never describes construction technique for ANY structure was not going to name a building material, so the absence is about the genre before it is about the architecture. (2) RV 6.2.7 'pleasant like an old man in a fort' and RV 9.107.10 'as a man enters the fort' are similes, and a simile draws on what its audience finds ordinary - so both PRESUPPOSE the inhabited fort the corpus never asserts (DJ-007). They are evidence FOR habitability extracted from the very passages a case against would cite. (3) pū́rpati- 'lord of the fort' at RV 1.173.10 names a political office attached to a púr. (4) Every result here is Grassmann's lexicon (DEP-005, DEP-021).
what_it_does_not_establish: It does not establish that Rigvedic púr- were small, temporary, or non-urban. It does not establish that brick was unknown to the composers. It does not settle whether púr- and the Harappan citadel are the same object - that is HYP-J-001, and the answer there is that this repository cannot tell.
falsifier: Falsified by a lemma glossed 'brick' or 'city' in a lexicon other than Grassmann's, which would also show the single-source dependency was doing the work. Substantially moved by Sāyaṇa or any pre-modern commentary on the ten material passages. Moved by an edition-based reading of the three locative passages that reads any of them as a statement rather than a simile.
notes: Written in this shape deliberately. The convenient version of this row - 'the Rigveda knows no cities, so pur is not Harappan' - is available, quotable, and not supported by the evidence assembled here. The preferred-counter-narrative test in 04-AUDITS/domain-j-method.md §5 caught an earlier draft of this row stating exactly that, and the two similes are what stopped it.

proposition: The English word 'fort' is not a translation of a Rigvedic category. It is a bracket that at least three different Sanskrit words fall into and out of depending on the century of the lexicon consulted.
evidence_for: durgá- is a fortress in Classical Sanskrit and is NOT one in these 21 Rigvedic passages on Grassmann's lexicon: all neuter, all difficult ground or peril, six of them one refrain, none broken or held (DJ-011). dehī́- 'Aufwurf, Damm, Wall' - an earth-heap from √dih 'smear, plaster up' - takes the same ninety-nine expression and the same opponent as púr- but is outside the register by an etymological rule (DJ-005). grā́ma-, glossed 'village' by habit, is a moving war-band in Grassmann's Rigvedic gloss (DJ-012). púr- itself is an earthwork or palisade, not a city.
evidence_against: Grassmann 1873 is one lexicographer, and a nineteenth-century German one whose glosses are themselves interpretive choices (DEP-005, DEP-021, RA-015). 'durgá- is not a fort in the Rigveda' is Grassmann's reading before it is a measurement, and a lexicon built on other principles could distribute these words differently. No second lexicon was reachable.
what_it_does_not_establish: It does not establish what any of these words did mean, only that the English bracket does not carry across them. It does not license replacing 'fort' with 'earthwork' as a new default gloss - that would repeat the error in the other direction.
falsifier: Falsified for durgá- by any Rigvedic passage where a durgá- is broken, besieged, entered or held; none of the 21 is. Falsified more generally by a second lexicon, or a pre-modern commentary, distributing these words as the English bracket does.
notes: §7 names 'fort' among the inherited English categories to audit before use. This is the audit's result at the level of the category rather than the single word: 06-BRIEFS/pur-translation-standard.md audits púr- under the full §7 block, and this row records that the audit does not stop at púr- because the English word does not.
